# Texas Solutions Truck Dispatch

> Texas Solutions is a US truck dispatch service for owner-operators and small fleets, based in Midland, Texas. Dispatch fee: 5% of weekly gross for OTR semi trucks, 7% for hotshots, 8% for box trucks and straight trucks. No flat rate, no setup fee, no monthly subscription, no forced loads. Also free trucking calculators (fuel cost, cost per mile, IFTA, HOS, load profitability and more), daily diesel prices by state, and a trucking blog. Texas Solutions is not a motor carrier or freight broker and does not guarantee loads, rates or earnings.

## Key facts
- Service: truck dispatch (load search, rate negotiation, broker setup packets, rate confirmations, lane planning)
- Semi truck dispatch fee (dry van, reefer, flatbed, step deck, power only): 5% of weekly gross, OTR - about $400-$500 per week on typical gross of $8,000-$10,000
- Hotshot dispatch fee: 7% of weekly gross, OTR - for example $490-$630 on a hypothetical $7,000-$9,000 week
- Box truck and straight truck dispatch fee: 8% of weekly gross, OTR - for example $560-$720 on a hypothetical $7,000-$9,000 week
- The fee is a percentage of weekly gross (what the truck earns hauling loads that week). No flat rate, no setup fee, no monthly subscription, no long-term contract, no forced loads
- Condition: Rates apply to OTR (over-the-road) operations. Local and regional work is quoted separately.
- Free trial: the first load is dispatched free
- Dispatchers available 24/7 (remote team across US time zones); works with brand-new MC authority from day one
- Back-office services: broker carrier packets, rate confirmations, invoicing and billing, detention and lumper collection, factoring setup, IFTA filing, DOT compliance help, MC authority setup
- Equipment dispatched: dry van, reefer, flatbed, step deck, power only, hotshot, box truck, straight truck
- Rough freight rates per mile (not guaranteed): flatbed $5-7, step deck $5-7, reefer $4-6, hotshot $4-5, dry van $3-5 (local or OTR), power only $3-5, box truck $1.80-3.20
- Area served: the United States (remote dispatchers across US time zones); office in Midland, Texas. Alaska and Hawaii-based carriers can ask about mainland operations
- Texas Solutions is a dispatch service. It is not a motor carrier or freight broker and does not guarantee loads, rates or earnings
- Phone: (838) 910-3147 | WhatsApp: +1 838 910 3147 (https://wa.me/18389103147) | Email: dispatch@texassolutions.co
- Address: 401 W Kentucky Ave, Midland, TX 79701
- Owner and CEO: Shehryar Joyia

## Free trucking calculators
- [Tools hub](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/): all calculators in one place
- [Dispatch fee calculator and free quote](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/dispatch-fee-calculator/): dispatch fee by truck type, plus a quote request via WhatsApp
- [Truck fuel cost calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/truck-fuel-cost-calculator/): MPG by truck type and load weight, trip fuel cost, cost per mile, daily diesel price by state
- [Cost Per Mile (CPM) Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/cost-per-mile-calculator/): Free trucking cost per mile calculator for owner-operators: fixed and variable costs, your own driver pay shown separately, and cost per total mile and per loaded mile.
- [Load Profitability Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/load-profitability-calculator/): Free load profitability calculator: revenue, dispatch and factoring fees, deadhead and return miles, your cost per mile and trip expenses give estimated profit, effective rate per mile and the rate you need.
- [Break-Even Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/break-even-calculator/): Free break-even calculator for owner-operators: enter fixed costs, variable cost per mile and your freight rate to see the miles per month you need to break even, and your profit at your planned miles.
- [Deadhead Miles Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/deadhead-miles-calculator/): Free deadhead miles calculator: see your deadhead percentage and effective rate per mile once empty miles are counted against a load's revenue.
- [Driver Pay Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/driver-pay-calculator/): Free truck driver pay calculator: work out weekly, monthly and annual pay for per-mile, per-load, percentage of gross, or hourly pay models.
- [IFTA Mileage Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/ifta-mileage-calculator/): Free IFTA mileage calculator: log miles driven and fuel purchased by state, see gallons consumed per jurisdiction, and estimate net taxable gallons for your own IFTA records.
- [Per Diem Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/per-diem-calculator/): Free per diem calculator for truck drivers: estimate your annual per diem deduction and potential tax savings based on days on the road. Not tax advice.
- [Truck Loan Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/truck-loan-calculator/): Free truck loan calculator: enter the truck price, down payment, interest rate and term to see your monthly payment, total interest and total cost.
- [Maintenance Budget Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/maintenance-budget-calculator/): Free truck maintenance budget calculator: estimate a yearly and monthly repair reserve based on your truck's age and annual mileage.
- [Hours of Service (HOS) Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/hours-of-service-calculator/): Free HOS calculator: estimate remaining drive time under the FMCSA 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour on-duty window and 60/7 or 70/8-day cycle limits. Planning tool only, not a legal record.
- [Freight Class Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/freight-class-calculator/): Free freight class calculator: estimate NMFC freight class from length, width, height and weight using the standard density table. Estimate only, confirm with your carrier.
- [Fuel Surcharge Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/fuel-surcharge-calculator/): Free trucking fuel surcharge calculator: base and current fuel price, agreed MPG and miles give surcharge per mile and total, using the per-mile, step-table or percentage method in your contract.
- [Detention Pay Calculator](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/calculators/detention-pay-calculator/): Free truck detention pay calculator: enter arrival, appointment and release times, free time, hourly rate and billing increment to see eligible detention hours and estimated detention pay.

## Guides (blog)
- [Working With a Factoring Company: Setup, Paperwork and Payments](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/working-with-a-factoring-company/): After onboarding, the factoring company sends a notice of assignment to your brokers so they pay the factor instead of you. For each load, you submit a clean packet (invoice, signed rate confirmation, signed BOL or POD and any receipts), get funded, and track which invoices are paid. Most problems come from missing paperwork, short pays and disputes, so a consistent routine matters.
- [Winter Driving and Chain Laws: A Trucker's Survival Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/winter-driving-and-chain-laws/): Chain laws are set by each state and can require trucks to carry chains during the winter season and put them on when conditions are posted. Before winter, learn the rules on your lanes, practice chaining up, prevent fuel gelling and frozen air lines, and carry an emergency kit. When conditions get dangerous, slow down or stop; no load is worth a crash.
- [Weigh Stations and Bypass: Weight Limits, Scales and Tips](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/weigh-stations-and-bypass/): Weigh stations check that trucks meet weight, size, safety and credential rules, and officers may pull trucks in for inspection. Bypass programs use a transponder or phone app to screen eligible trucks on the approach and may signal you to pass if your safety record and credentials qualify. You must still follow posted signs and pull in whenever directed.
- [UCR Registration Guide: Who Needs It, Fees and Deadlines](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/ucr-registration-guide/): Unified Carrier Registration (UCR) is a yearly federal-state registration program for businesses involved in interstate commerce, including most for-hire and private interstate motor carriers, brokers, freight forwarders and leasing companies. Carriers pay a fee based on the size of their fleet. You register for each calendar year, and states can enforce it at roadside.
- [TWIC Card and Port Drayage: A Guide for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/twic-card-and-port-drayage/): Yes, in most cases. A TWIC card from TSA is required for unescorted access to secure areas of ports and other maritime facilities, which is where container pickups and drop-offs happen. Drayage carriers also usually need an intermodal interchange agreement, terminal registration and the right insurance before they can pull a container.
- [Trucking Tax Basics for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-tax-basics/): Most owner-operators deal with federal income tax, self-employment tax, often state income tax, plus trucking-specific taxes like the Heavy Vehicle Use Tax (Form 2290) and fuel tax through IFTA. Because no employer withholds for you, you usually pay estimated taxes during the year. A CPA who works with trucking businesses should confirm what applies to you.
- [Trucking LLC Setup and Simple Bookkeeping for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-llc-and-bookkeeping/): Many owner-operators form an LLC to separate business and personal affairs, though an LLC does not replace insurance and its protection has limits. Whatever entity you choose, keep a separate business bank account, record every load and expense weekly, and reconcile monthly. An attorney and a CPA should confirm the right structure for you.
- [Trucking KPIs to Track: 10 Numbers That Run Your Business](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-kpis-to-track/): Start with revenue per total mile, cost per mile, profit per mile, deadhead percentage, miles and revenue per truck per week, fuel economy, maintenance cost per mile and average days to get paid. Track them weekly, compare them over time, and use them to decide which loads, lanes and brokers are worth your truck.
- [Trucking Insurance Explained: Coverages Owner-Operators Need](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-insurance-explained/): A carrier with its own authority usually needs primary auto liability (filed with FMCSA), cargo coverage that most brokers and shippers require, and physical damage coverage to protect the truck, especially if it is financed. Leased-on drivers often need non-trucking liability instead. Exact needs depend on your operation, so review them with a licensed insurance agent.
- [How to Write a Trucking Business Plan (With a Simple Template)](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-business-plan/): A useful trucking business plan covers your business summary, the freight and lanes you will run, your equipment, how you will find loads, your startup costs, a monthly operating budget, revenue and break-even projections, and your compliance and growth plans. Keep it short, realistic and built on your own cost per mile.
- [Trucking Apps for Owner-Operators: What You Actually Need](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-apps-for-owner-operators/): Most owner-operators rely on a few core app types: a truck-specific GPS, an ELD that is on FMCSA's registered list, a load board, a document scanning tool, and a way to track expenses and miles for taxes and IFTA. Fuel, parking, weather and weigh station apps are useful extras. Choose by features, cost and how well the tools work together.
- [Truck Parking and Trip Planning: How to Never Get Stuck](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-parking-and-trip-planning/): Work backward from your hours of service: figure out where your 11 hours of driving or 14-hour window will run out, then pick a primary parking spot well before that point plus one or two backups. Aim to park before evening when lots fill up, use reserved parking when the stakes are high, and ask shippers and receivers about overnight parking ahead of time.
- [Truck Maintenance Schedule for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-maintenance-schedule/): Combine daily pre-trip and post-trip checks, weekly and monthly walk-around inspections, preventive maintenance (PM) services at the intervals your engine and component makers recommend, and at least the annual inspection that FMCSA requires. Keep written records of everything, and set aside money each mile for repairs and tires.
- [TONU, Layover and Lumper Pay: How Truckers Get Paid for Each](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/tonu-layover-and-lumper-pay/): TONU (truck ordered not used) pays the carrier when a booked load is cancelled after the truck was dispatched. Layover pays for an extra day when a load cannot be picked up or delivered as scheduled, and lumper pay reimburses the fee charged to unload freight. Each should be agreed on the rate confirmation and backed by proof to get paid.
- [Team Driving in Trucking: Pay, Hours and How to Make It Work](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/team-driving-guide/): Two drivers share one truck and take turns driving while the other rests in the sleeper berth, so the truck can keep moving close to around the clock. Each driver follows their own hours of service limits and keeps their own log. Teams can run far more miles per week than a solo driver, which suits time-sensitive and long-haul freight. Confirm current hours of service rules with FMCSA.
- [How to Start a Cargo Van Business: A Practical Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/start-a-cargo-van-business/): Pick a freight model first (local courier, contract routes or long-distance expedite), then buy a van that fits it, form a business entity, get the right registrations and commercial insurance, and track your cost per mile before you take rates. Interstate for-hire hauling generally needs FMCSA operating authority, so confirm your exact requirements with FMCSA and your state before you start.
- [Sleeper Berth Split Explained: 7/3 and 8/2 With Examples](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/sleeper-berth-split-explained/): Property-carrying drivers can split their required 10 hours off duty into two periods: one of at least 7 hours in the sleeper berth and one of at least 2 hours off duty or in the sleeper, totaling at least 10 hours. When the two periods are paired, neither counts against the 14-hour window, and you recalculate your hours from the end of the first period. Confirm current rules with FMCSA.
- [Reefer Loads in Summer Heat: How to Protect the Load](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/reefer-loads-in-summer-heat/): Pre-cool the trailer to the set point before loading, check product pulp temperatures and note warm product on the bill of lading, load for good airflow, run the mode the shipper requires, and keep doors closed and fuel topped off. Download or record the temperature history so you can prove the load was kept in range.
- [Reefer Loads and Refrigerated Load Dispatch: Rates per Mile, Seasons and Tips](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/reefer-loads-guide/): Our dispatchers plan reefer freight at roughly $4 to $6 a mile (October 2026 planning range, not a market index or quote). Real reefer rates depend on the lane, the season, distance and how much outbound freight the delivery market has. Produce season and the holiday peak usually push reefer demand and rates up.
- [Pre-Trip Inspection Checklist for Truck Drivers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/pre-trip-inspection-checklist/): A pre-trip inspection covers the engine compartment, cab and gauges, air brake system, lights and reflectors, tires and wheels, suspension, coupling devices and the trailer, plus the emergency equipment and documents in the cab. Federal rules require the driver to be satisfied the vehicle is in safe operating condition before driving. Use your state CDL manual and FMCSA rules for the current required items.
- [Power Only Trucking Explained: How It Works and Who It Fits](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/power-only-trucking-explained/): Power only trucking is when a carrier supplies the tractor and driver, and the shipper, broker or another company supplies the trailer. You hook to a preloaded trailer, haul it, and drop it at the destination. It lets owner-operators haul freight without buying a trailer, but you need the right insurance for trailers you do not own.
- [How to Plan a Profitable Round Trip in Trucking](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/plan-a-profitable-round-trip/): Price the whole loop instead of a single load: check how strong the outbound market is at the delivery city before you accept the first leg, add all loaded and empty miles, and compare the total revenue to your cost per mile. If the return market is weak, ask more for the first leg or build a triangle route that keeps the truck loaded.
- [PHMSA Hazmat Registration: Who Needs It and How to File](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/phmsa-hazmat-registration/): Carriers and shippers that offer or transport certain hazardous materials in commerce, most commonly any shipment that requires placards, must register with PHMSA each registration year, which runs July 1 to June 30. You file online, pay a fee based on business size, and keep a copy of the certificate or the registration number in each truck. Confirm current thresholds and fees with PHMSA.
- [Personal Conveyance and Yard Moves: When You Can Use Them](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/personal-conveyance-and-yard-moves/): Personal conveyance is moving your truck for personal reasons while off duty, such as driving from a shipper to the nearest safe place to rest or from your hotel to a restaurant, as long as the move does not advance the load or the business. Yard moves are on-duty, not-driving moves inside a yard or similar area with restricted public access. Your carrier must allow both, and FMCSA guidance sets the limits.
- [Peak Season Trucking Loads: How Owner-Operators Can Plan Q4 Holiday Freight](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/peak-season-trucking/): Q4 peak season brings retail, holiday food and e-commerce freight, mostly in October to December. Owner-operators do best by positioning near big distribution markets, booking reloads before they deliver, negotiating harder on short-notice freight and planning home time early, because rates and demand can swing quickly around Thanksgiving and Christmas.
- [Owner-Operator vs Company Driver: Which Path Is Right for You?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/owner-operator-vs-company-driver/): A company driver earns a steadier paycheck with fewer costs and less risk, while an owner-operator can earn more but pays for the truck, fuel, insurance and repairs and carries all the business risk. Becoming an owner-operator makes sense when you have savings, know your cost per mile and want to run a business, not just drive.
- [Oversize and Overweight Permits: A Practical Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/oversize-overweight-permits/): You need a permit from each state you drive through when your load exceeds that state's legal width, height, length or weight limits. Permits are generally only issued for non-divisible loads, and they come with route, time-of-day and sometimes escort requirements. Each state sets its own rules, so check with every state's permit office on your route.
- [Out-of-Service Criteria: What Puts a Truck or Driver Out of Service](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/out-of-service-criteria/): Out of service means an inspector has found a problem serious enough that the driver may not drive, or the vehicle may not be operated, until it is fixed. The rules come from the CVSA North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria. OOS violations carry extra weight in your CSA data and can cost you the load, so prevention matters.
- [New Entrant Safety Audit: How to Prepare and Pass](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/new-entrant-safety-audit-guide/): The new entrant safety audit is a review FMCSA conducts during a new motor carrier's first 18 months to confirm it has basic safety management controls in place. Auditors look at driver qualification, drug and alcohol testing, hours of service, vehicle maintenance, insurance and accident records. Certain violations cause an automatic fail, so have every file ready before the audit notice arrives and confirm current procedures with FMCSA.
- [DOT Physical and Medical Card: What Truck Drivers Should Know](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/medical-card-and-dot-physical/): A DOT medical examiner's certificate is valid for up to 24 months. The examiner can issue a shorter card, often one year or less, when a condition such as high blood pressure or insulin-treated diabetes needs closer monitoring. Confirm current standards with FMCSA, and renew before the expiration date to avoid losing driving privileges.
- [Load-to-Truck Ratio Explained for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/load-to-truck-ratio-explained/): The load-to-truck ratio compares the number of loads posted on a load board to the number of trucks posted for the same equipment type and area. A higher ratio means more freight competing for each truck, which usually supports higher spot rates; a lower ratio means more trucks chasing each load and more pressure on rates.
- [Lease vs Buy a Truck: Which Is Better for Owner-Operators?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/lease-vs-buy-a-truck/): Buying usually costs less over the long run and builds equity, but you carry repair risk and need more cash upfront. Leasing can lower upfront cost and, with full-service leases, bundle maintenance, but you build little or no equity and must follow the lease terms. The right choice depends on your cash, credit, miles and how long you plan to keep the truck.
- [How to Keep Your MC Authority Active and in Good Standing](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/keep-your-mc-authority-active/): Keep the required liability insurance on file with FMCSA without gaps, keep a valid BOC-3 process agent filing, update your MCS-150 every two years and whenever your information changes, and register for UCR each year. Stay enrolled in a drug and alcohol testing program and keep your safety records clean, because a lapse in any of these can lead to revocation, deactivation or brokers refusing to load you.
- [How to Vet a Freight Broker Before You Haul Their Load](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker/): Look up the broker's MC number with FMCSA to confirm active broker authority and a bond or trust on file, then check their credit and average days to pay. Verify contact details against official records, read the broker-carrier agreement for payment, claims and fine terms, and watch for red flags like off-market rates or pressure to skip paperwork.
- [How to Read a Rate Confirmation Before You Sign It](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation/): Read a rate confirmation top to bottom before signing: confirm the broker's legal name and MC number, the pickup and delivery details, the commodity and weight, and the total rate. Then check the accessorial terms (detention, TONU, lumper, layover), the payment terms and any fines or tracking rules in the fine print. If anything differs from what you agreed on the phone, get it corrected in writing first.
- [How to Get Loads With a New MC Number: A Guide for New Authority Carriers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-loads-with-new-mc-number/): Prepare one complete broker setup packet (MC authority, W-9, certificate of insurance and notice of assignment if you factor), get set up with brokers that accept new authority before you need a load, start on lanes and load boards where new carriers get booked, and deliver every load on time so brokers rebook you. A dispatcher who works with new authority can do the searching and setups while you drive.
- [How to Get Detention Paid: A Step-by-Step Guide for Carriers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-detention-paid/): Get detention terms (free time and hourly rate) written on the rate confirmation before pickup, then document exact arrival and departure times with signed paperwork. Notify the broker in writing as soon as free time is about to run out, and invoice detention with your proof right after delivery. Carriers who skip any of these steps get denied far more often.
- [How to Finance a Semi Truck: A Step-by-Step Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-finance-a-semi-truck/): Most owner-operators finance a semi with an equipment loan secured by the truck itself. Lenders look at your credit, time in business, driving experience, down payment and the truck's age and mileage. Get several written offers, compare the total cost over the full term, and make sure the payment fits your real cost per mile.
- [How to File Form 2290: Heavy Vehicle Use Tax for Truckers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-file-form-2290/): File IRS Form 2290 for each heavy vehicle with a taxable gross weight at or above the IRS threshold, usually by e-filing through an IRS-authorized provider. The return covers a July-to-June tax period and is generally due by the end of the month after the month the truck is first used on public highways. Keep the stamped Schedule 1, because you need it to register or renew plates.
- [How to Dispute a Roadside Violation With DataQs](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-dispute-a-violation-dataqs/): Create a DataQs account, file a Request for Data Review on the specific inspection or crash, explain clearly what is wrong, and attach evidence such as repair receipts, ELD records, photos or court documents. The request goes to the agency that owns the record, usually the state that did the inspection, which decides whether to change it.
- [How to Choose an ELD: Features and Questions to Ask](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-an-eld/): Start by confirming the device is on FMCSA's registered ELD list and not on the revoked list. Then compare hardware fit for your truck, how easy the driver app is, how edits and unidentified driving are handled, total cost including hardware and contract terms, and the quality of support. Choose the one that fits your operation, not the one with the longest feature list.
- [How to Choose a Factoring Company: Features and Questions to Ask](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-a-factoring-company/): Compare factoring companies on the total cost per invoice (rate plus every extra fee), recourse terms, advance rate, contract length and exit terms, funding speed and broker credit tools. Read the full contract, ask how they handle disputes and termination, and pick the one whose terms fit your cash flow, not just the lowest headline rate.
- [Hiring Your First Truck Driver: A Step-by-Step Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/hiring-your-first-truck-driver/): Run the numbers first to confirm a second truck will earn enough to pay a driver, then get the driver approved by your insurance agent, complete the DQ file, pre-employment drug test and Clearinghouse query, and agree on a written pay plan. Decide on employee versus contractor status with a CPA or attorney before the first paycheck. Confirm current FMCSA qualification rules before the driver's first load.
- [Hazmat Endorsement Guide for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/hazmat-endorsement-guide/): First-time applicants complete hazmat theory training from a registered ELDT provider, pass a TSA security threat assessment with fingerprints, and pass the state hazmat knowledge test. Once the state receives TSA approval and your test results, it adds the H endorsement to your CDL. Confirm current steps and fees with your state licensing agency and TSA.
- [How to Grow From 1 to 5 Trucks Without Breaking Your Business](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/grow-from-1-to-5-trucks/): Grow one truck at a time, and only after your first truck shows steady profit per mile, you have cash reserves and you have systems for dispatch, maintenance, compliance and payroll. Each truck you add should be able to pay for itself, its driver and its share of overhead on realistic rates, not your best weeks.
- [Fuel-Saving Tips for Truckers: Cut Your Diesel Bill](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/fuel-saving-tips-for-truckers/): The biggest fuel savers are usually driving a steady, moderate speed, cutting idle time, keeping tires properly inflated, maintaining the engine and aerodynamic parts, and planning routes and fuel stops to avoid empty miles and high-priced pumps. Small mpg gains add up to real money over a year of driving.
- [Freight Market Calendar: Busy and Slow Months for Truckers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/freight-market-calendar/): Freight usually softens in January and February, builds through spring produce season, tightens around holidays and quarter ends, and peaks in late summer and fall as retailers stock for the holidays. The exact timing varies by region, equipment type and the wider economy, so use the calendar as a planning guide, not a guarantee.
- [Flatbed Cargo Securement: Rules, Math and a Checklist](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/flatbed-cargo-securement/): Two things must both be true: the combined working load limit of your tiedowns must be at least half the cargo's weight, and you need a minimum number of tiedowns based on each article's length and weight. For an article over 10 feet that is not blocked at the front, that is two tiedowns for the first 10 feet plus one for each additional 10 feet or part of it. Check FMCSA's cargo securement rules for the details and commodity-specific requirements.
- [How to Start a Final Mile Delivery Business](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/final-mile-delivery-business/): A final mile business delivers goods on the last leg from a warehouse or hub to a home or business, often with a box truck and a two-person crew. Most carriers work under contracts with logistics companies or retailers and are paid per stop, per route or per day. Profit depends on route density, damage rates and labor costs.
- [Expedited Freight: How It Works and How to Haul It](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/expedited-freight-guide/): Expedited freight is time-critical cargo that must move faster than normal service, usually in a dedicated vehicle that goes straight from pickup to delivery with no other stops. It is hauled by vans, straight trucks, hotshots and team-driven semis. It often pays more per mile, but you may wait unpaid between loads.
- [Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT): What New CDL Drivers Need](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/entry-level-driver-training-eldt/): Since February 7, 2022, people getting a Class A or Class B CDL for the first time, upgrading from Class B to Class A, or getting a first-time hazmat, passenger or school bus endorsement generally must complete ELDT from a provider listed on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry before testing. Drivers who already held those credentials before that date are generally not affected. Confirm current rules and exceptions with FMCSA.
- [ELD Malfunction Rules: What to Do When Your ELD Fails](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/eld-malfunction-rules/): Note the malfunction, notify your motor carrier in writing within 24 hours, and switch to paper logs, reconstructing the current day and the previous 7 days if the ELD cannot show them. The carrier generally has 8 days to repair or replace the device unless FMCSA grants an extension. Confirm current details in FMCSA's ELD rule (49 CFR 395.34).
- [DOT Drug and Alcohol Testing Program for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/drug-and-alcohol-testing-program/): Write or adopt a testing policy, join a consortium or third-party administrator so you are in a random testing pool, register in the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse and designate your administrator, and complete a pre-employment drug test and Clearinghouse query before driving. After that, keep up with random tests, annual queries and records. Confirm current rules in 49 CFR Parts 382 and 40 with FMCSA.
- [Driver Qualification File Checklist for Small Carriers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/driver-qualification-file-checklist/): A driver qualification (DQ) file holds the documents that prove a driver is qualified to operate a commercial motor vehicle: the employment application, motor vehicle records, previous employer safety history, road test or CDL equivalent, medical certificate with examiner verification, and annual reviews. Interstate carriers must keep one for every driver, including an owner-operator who drives for their own authority. Confirm the current list in 49 CFR Part 391 on the FMCSA website.
- [Double Brokering and Freight Fraud: How Carriers Protect Themselves](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/double-brokering-and-freight-fraud/): Double brokering is when a party re-brokers a load to another carrier without authorization, often using a stolen or fake identity, and then disappears with the payment. Carriers avoid it by verifying every broker's authority and contact details independently, confirming the load with the real broker and shipper, never paying fees to get loads, and securing their own FMCSA, email and load board accounts.
- [DOT Roadside Inspections: Levels, What Officers Check, How to Pass](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dot-roadside-inspections/): An officer checks the driver, the vehicle or both, depending on the inspection level. A Level I inspection is the most complete and covers the driver's license, medical certificate, hours of service and paperwork plus a hands-on check of brakes, tires, lights, coupling and cargo securement. Violations are recorded and count toward your CSA data, and serious ones can place the driver or truck out of service.
- [Load Board vs Dispatcher: Should You Self-Dispatch or Hire a Truck Dispatcher?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dispatcher-vs-self-dispatch-load-board/): Self-dispatching from a load board saves the dispatch fee but costs hours every day in searching, calling brokers and paperwork. A dispatcher is worth it when better rates, fewer deadhead miles and the time you get back are worth more than the fee. Many owner-operators self-dispatch at first, then hire a dispatcher once phone time starts cutting into driving time.
- [CSA Scores Explained: How FMCSA Measures Your Safety](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/csa-scores-explained/): CSA scores are percentiles that FMCSA's Safety Measurement System calculates from your roadside inspections, violations and crashes, grouped into categories called BASICs. Recent and more severe violations count more, and the score compares you to carriers of similar size. High percentiles can lead to warning letters, investigations and fewer brokers willing to load you.
- [Crossing Into Canada and Mexico: A Trucker's Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/crossing-into-canada-and-mexico/): You need a valid passport or other accepted travel document such as a FAST card, a clean admissibility record, a carrier code and a way to file Canada's advance eManifest, insurance that covers Canada, and your IFTA and IRP credentials set up for the provinces you will run. Canada also has its own hours of service and ELD rules. Confirm current requirements with CBSA, CBP and your insurance agent before booking.
- [Cheapest Truck Dispatch Service? How to Compare Dispatch Fees and Their Real Cost](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/cheapest-truck-dispatch-service/): The cheapest truck dispatch service is the one with the lowest total cost for your truck, not the lowest advertised number. Add up the percentage or weekly fee, any setup fee, minimum, contract term and extra charges for paperwork, then compare what each fee includes. A percentage of weekly gross costs nothing in a week the truck does not run; a flat weekly fee does.
- [Carrier Packet Checklist: Documents Brokers Ask For](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/carrier-packet-checklist/): A carrier packet usually includes your operating authority (MC) letter, a W-9, a certificate of insurance naming the broker as certificate holder, a signed broker-carrier agreement, and payment details such as a voided check or a factoring notice of assignment. Keeping these current and ready to send gets you set up with brokers faster.
- [Cargo Claims Guide: How to Prevent, Handle and Settle Them](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/cargo-claims-guide/): Prevent claims by inspecting and documenting freight at pickup, noting exceptions on the bill of lading and protecting the seal. If damage or shortage happens, document everything at delivery, notify the broker and your insurer quickly, and respond to the written claim with your records. Talk to your insurance agent or an attorney about liability questions on larger claims.
- [Buying a Used Semi Truck: Inspection Checklist and Red Flags](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/buying-a-used-semi-truck/): Check the paperwork (title, liens, VIN match), the maintenance and repair history, an ECM report, an oil analysis, the emissions system and the frame, tires and brakes, and have an independent heavy-truck mechanic inspect it before you pay. Budget for repairs after purchase, because almost every used truck needs some.
- [Box Truck vs Cargo Van: Which Is Better for Your Business?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/box-truck-vs-cargo-van/): A cargo van costs less to buy and run and has fewer rules, but carries small loads at lower rates. A box truck costs more and brings more compliance work, but it hauls pallets and liftgate freight that opens up more customers. Choose based on the freight you can reliably get, not on the vehicle alone.
- [BOC-3 Filing Explained: Process Agents for Trucking Authority](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/boc-3-filing-explained/): A BOC-3 is the FMCSA form that designates a process agent in each state where a carrier, broker or freight forwarder operates. A process agent is the person or company that can accept legal papers on your behalf in that state. FMCSA requires it before granting operating authority, and most carriers have a blanket process agent company file it electronically.
- [Best Truck Dispatch Service for Owner-Operators in 2026: How to Compare](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/best-truck-dispatch-service/): The best truck dispatch service is the one that fits your truck and authority: a clear fee with nothing hidden, no long-term contract, no forced dispatch, experience with your equipment, help with broker paperwork and real people you can reach 24/7. Compare the total cost and the service included, not only the percentage.
- [Truck Loads and Load Boards: How They Work for Carriers](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-loads-and-load-boards-guide/): A load board is an online marketplace where brokers and shippers post truck loads and carriers search for freight that fits their equipment and lanes. Carriers filter by origin, destination, equipment and date, check the broker's credit and payment history, then call or message to negotiate and book. Paid boards like DAT and Truckstop add more loads and tools, while free boards have fewer features.
- [Non-CDL Box Truck and Hotshot Loads: Weight Rules and How to Find Freight](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/non-cdl-box-truck-and-hotshot-loads/): Often yes, if you stay under the federal CDL thresholds. A single truck generally needs a CDL at a GVWR or actual weight of 26,001 lbs or more, and a combination generally needs a Class A CDL at 26,001 lbs or more combined when the trailer is rated or weighs over 10,000 lbs. Placarded hazmat requires a CDL at any size. Confirm with FMCSA and your state before you buy or load.
- [How to Start a Hotshot Business: Truck, Trailer, Authority and Dispatch](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-start-a-hotshot-business/): Pick a heavy-duty pickup and flatbed or gooseneck trailer that match the freight you plan to haul, check whether the combination's weight ratings require a CDL, then get a USDOT number, MC operating authority, a BOC-3 and commercial insurance. Once your authority is active, book loads through load boards, brokers or a hotshot dispatch company.
- [How to Start a Box Truck Business: Authority, Equipment and First Loads](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-start-a-box-truck-business/): Choose a box truck that fits the freight you want (most owner-operators pick a 26 ft truck with a liftgate), form your business, get a USDOT number and MC operating authority, file a BOC-3, and buy the insurance brokers require. Then set up invoicing and start booking loads through load boards, brokers or a dispatcher who works with new authority.
- [How to Get Loads Without a Broker: Direct Freight Explained](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-loads-without-a-broker/): Owner-operators get loads without a broker by working directly with shippers, winning dedicated lanes or contracts, and using carrier platforms such as Amazon Relay. Direct freight can pay more and be steadier, but it takes time to win, often pays on longer terms, and usually requires a clean safety record and proven on-time service.
- [How to Choose a Fuel Card for Truckers: What to Compare](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-a-fuel-card-for-truckers/): Start with where you actually fuel, then compare how the discount is calculated (retail-minus or cost-plus), which truck stops accept the card, every fee, whether it is credit or prepaid, and how well it reports gallons by state for IFTA. The best fuel card for truckers is the one that fits your lanes and paperwork, not the one with the biggest advertised number.
- [How to Become an Owner-Operator: Lease-On or Your Own MC](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-become-an-owner-operator/): To become an owner-operator you need the right license and experience for your truck, a truck you own or lease, and a way to haul freight: either leasing on to an existing carrier or getting your own USDOT number and MC authority. Running your own MC also means insurance, broker setup, compliance and a plan for finding loads, which is where a dispatch service can help.
- [How Much Do Hotshot Drivers Make? A Realistic Look at Gross and Net](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-much-do-hotshot-drivers-make/): Hotshot owner-operator income depends on miles, rates and costs. As a hypothetical example, hotshots might gross about $7,000 to $9,000 a week, which is not guaranteed. After fuel, insurance, equipment payments, maintenance and fees, our worked examples keep about 51 to 59 percent of gross before taxes, and real results can be lower.
- [How Much Do Box Truck Owner-Operators Make? Gross, Costs and Net](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-much-do-box-truck-owner-operators-make/): It varies widely with miles, rates and costs. As a hypothetical example, box trucks might gross about $7,000 to $9,000 a week, though that is not guaranteed. After fuel, insurance, truck payments, maintenance and fees, our worked examples keep about 44 to 51 percent of gross before taxes, and real results can be lower.
- [How Does Truck Dispatching Work? A Carrier's Step-by-Step Guide](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-does-truck-dispatching-work/): A truck dispatcher works for the carrier, not the shipper. After onboarding your authority, insurance and preferences, the dispatcher searches for loads that fit your truck and lanes, negotiates the rate with the broker, and books the load only after you approve it. The dispatcher then handles paperwork, check calls and invoicing support, and charges a fee, usually a percentage of the truck's weekly gross.
- [Freight Dispatcher vs Truck Dispatcher: Same Job, Different Name](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/freight-dispatcher-vs-truck-dispatcher/): For a US carrier, yes. Freight dispatcher, truck dispatcher, trucking dispatcher and cargo dispatcher are different labels for the same carrier-side role: someone who finds loads for your truck, negotiates the rate, and books freight under your authority after you approve it. The real differences to watch are who the person works for and what services the fee includes, not the job title.
- [Dry Van, Reefer, Flatbed and Power Only Loads: Finding and Pricing Them](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dry-van-reefer-flatbed-power-only-loads/): Rate per mile depends on the lane, season, distance, how much equipment is available in the pickup market, and the extra work or cost the load involves. Flatbed and step deck usually pay more for securement and tarping, reefer pays more for temperature control, and dry van and power only face the most competition. All rates vary and are not guaranteed.
- [Dispatch Service Percentage vs Flat Fee: Which Is Better?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dispatch-percentage-vs-flat-fee/): A percentage fee rises and falls with what your truck earns, so you pay less in slow weeks and the dispatcher is motivated to book better-paying freight. A flat fee is predictable but costs the same in a bad week. The right choice depends on your weekly gross, how steady your freight is, and whether the offer hides extra charges or contracts.
- [Box Truck Contracts: How to Get Them and Where Amazon Relay Fits](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/box-truck-contracts-how-to-get-them/): Most box truck contracts grow out of a track record: on-time spot loads that turn into repeat lanes with brokers, then dedicated or contract work with brokers, shippers and local businesses. Have your authority, insurance and paperwork ready, approach shippers whose freight fits a box truck, and protect your service record. Amazon Relay is another option for carriers with their own authority who meet its current requirements.
- [Best Load Boards for Hotshot and How to Find Hotshot Loads](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/best-load-boards-for-hotshot/): No single load board is best for every hotshot. Large boards such as DAT, Truckstop and 123Loadboard all carry hotshot and partial flatbed freight, and the right one depends on your lanes, deck length and weight limits. Test a board, track the loads you actually book and what they pay, and keep the one that earns its cost.
- [Best Load Boards for Box Trucks and How to Find Box Truck Loads](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/best-load-boards-for-box-trucks/): There is no single best load board for every box truck. Large general boards such as DAT, Truckstop and 123Loadboard all let you filter for straight or box truck freight, and the right choice depends on the lanes you run and how much box truck freight shows up there. Many owner-operators test a board for a month, track the loads they actually book, and keep the one that pays.
- [Is a Truck Dispatcher Worth It? Self-Dispatch vs Dispatch Service](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/is-a-truck-dispatcher-worth-it/): A truck dispatcher is worth it when the fee costs less than the value you get back in better rates, fewer empty miles, less paperwork and more time to drive or rest. If you already have strong broker relationships and enjoy booking freight, self-dispatch can work well. Compare the fee with your own time and results before you decide.
- [How to Start a Trucking Company and Get Loads With New Authority](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-start-a-trucking-company/): Register with FMCSA for a USDOT number and MC operating authority, file a BOC-3, register for UCR, get the required insurance, and set up IRP plates, IFTA, an ELD and a drug and alcohol program where they apply. Then set up factoring and broker accounts. With new authority, expect some brokers to say no at first, and focus on those that accept new carriers.
- [How to Negotiate Freight Rates and Increase Your Rate Per Mile](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates/): Know your cost per mile and your minimum rate before you call. Ask about the load details, counter above your target with a clear reason, and be ready to walk away. Include deadhead miles in your math so the rate covers every mile you drive.
- [How to Find Loads for Your Truck: A Practical Guide for Owner-Operators](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-find-loads-for-your-truck/): Most owner-operators find loads through a mix of load boards, direct broker relationships, direct shippers and dispatch services. The highest paying loads are usually the ones that pay well per total mile, including deadhead, and leave you in a market with good outbound freight. A dispatcher can search, negotiate and book loads for you under your own authority.
- [How to Choose a Truck Dispatcher and Avoid Dispatch Scams](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-a-truck-dispatcher/): Check that the dispatcher has a real business presence, a written agreement, clear fees and no upfront payment demands. Ask for references from current carriers and look at independent reviews. Walk away from anyone who guarantees income, asks you to haul under their authority or pressures you to accept loads.
- [How Much Do Owner-Operators Make? Gross vs Net Explained](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-much-do-owner-operators-make/): It varies widely. What an owner-operator makes is weekly gross minus fuel, truck costs, insurance, maintenance, fees and taxes. In our example, a semi grossing $7,200 in a week keeps about $3,000 before taxes. Your own result depends on your rate per mile, miles, costs and home time.
- [Broker Setup, Rate Confirmations and Spot vs Contract Rates](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/broker-setup-spot-vs-contract/): To get set up with a broker, a carrier completes the broker's carrier packet, usually online. It typically includes your MC authority, certificate of insurance, W-9, a signed broker-carrier agreement and payment details. Once approved, the broker can send you a rate confirmation for a load.
- [What Is Deadhead in Trucking and How to Reduce It](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/what-is-deadhead-in-trucking/): Deadhead is driving a truck empty, without paid freight, usually to reach a pickup or return from a delivery. Deadhead miles burn fuel and use up legal driving hours while earning nothing, so they lower your effective rate per mile. You can cut them by planning the next load before you deliver, and by choosing lanes with strong return freight.
- [What Is a Good Rate Per Mile in Trucking in 2026?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/what-is-a-good-rate-per-mile/): A good rate per mile is one that covers your total cost per mile, including deadhead, and leaves profit. As a rough guide in 2026, flatbed and step deck often pay about $5-7 a mile, reefer $4-6, hotshot $4-5, dry van and power only $3-5, and box trucks $1.80-3.20, depending on lane, season and market.
- [Truck Dispatcher vs Freight Broker: The Real Difference](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-dispatcher-vs-freight-broker/): A truck dispatcher works for the carrier: they find and negotiate loads for the carrier's trucks and are paid by the carrier, usually a percentage of gross. A freight broker works between shippers and carriers: they need their own FMCSA broker authority and a surety bond, and earn the margin between what the shipper pays and what the carrier is paid.
- [How to Get Your MC Number and Trucking Authority](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-an-mc-number/): To get an MC number you register with FMCSA for a USDOT number, apply for for-hire operating authority (the MC number), file a BOC-3 process agent, and have your insurer file proof of at least $750,000 liability coverage for general freight. Authority typically goes active a few weeks after everything is on file.
- [IFTA for Owner-Operators: How to File Quarterly Returns](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-file-ifta/): The International Fuel Tax Agreement (IFTA) lets carriers running across US states and Canadian provinces file one quarterly fuel tax return with their base jurisdiction. Returns are due the last day of the month after each quarter ends: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31.
- [Hours of Service Rules Explained: 11, 14 and 70-Hour](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/hours-of-service-rules/): Property-carrying drivers may drive up to 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty, may not drive beyond the 14th hour after coming on duty, must take a 30-minute break after 8 cumulative hours of driving, and cannot drive after 60 hours in 7 days or 70 hours in 8 days. A 34-hour off-duty restart resets the weekly cycle.
- [Freight Factoring for Owner-Operators: How It Works](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/freight-factoring-explained/): In freight factoring, you sell your unpaid invoices to a factoring company, which advances you most of the invoice value right away, often 80-95%, and pays the rest, minus its fee, when the broker pays. Fees commonly run from about 1% to 5% of the invoice, depending on volume, terms and whether the deal is recourse or non-recourse.
- [Dry Van vs Reefer vs Flatbed: Which Trailer Pays Best?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dry-van-vs-reefer-vs-flatbed/): As a rough guide, flatbed and step deck loads often pay about $5-7 a mile, reefer about $4-6, and dry van about $3-5, depending on lane, season and whether the run is local or OTR. Higher rates come with more work: tarping and securement on flatbed, temperature and appointment rules on reefer. Dry van has the most freight and the most competition.
- [Cost of Running a Semi Truck Per Mile (2026 Breakdown)](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/cost-of-running-a-semi-truck-per-mile/): The American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI) found the industry-average cost to operate a truck in 2025 was $2.336 per mile, or $1.854 per mile excluding fuel. Your own cost depends on your truck payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance and how many miles you run, so calculate it yourself before accepting rates.
- [Best Load Boards for Owner-Operators and How to Use Them](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/best-load-boards-for-owner-operators/): Popular load boards include DAT One, Truckstop and 123Loadboard, plus specialty boards for hotshot, flatbed and power only. The best one depends on your equipment and lanes: look for fresh postings, rate data, broker credit information, and easy filtering. Many carriers use two boards and vet every broker before booking.
- [How Much Does a Truck Dispatcher Cost in 2026?](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-much-does-a-truck-dispatcher-cost/): Most independent truck dispatchers charge a percentage of the truck's weekly gross, usually somewhere between 3% and 10%. Texas Solutions charges 5% for OTR semi trucks, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks and straight trucks, with no flat rate, no setup fee and no monthly subscription.
- [Hotshot Trucking Rates Per Mile, Fuel and Dispatch (2026)](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/hotshot-trucking-rates/): Hotshot loads often pay roughly $4 to $5 a mile, depending on lane, urgency and season. A 1-ton diesel pulling a gooseneck typically gets about 13-14 mpg empty and 8-10 mpg loaded. Texas Solutions dispatches hotshots for 7% of weekly gross, OTR, with no flat rate.
- [Diesel Prices by State: How Truckers Cut Fuel Cost Per Mile](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/cut-fuel-cost-per-mile/): Fuel cost per mile equals the diesel price divided by your miles per gallon. A loaded semi averaging about 6.3 mpg with diesel at $6.00 a gallon spends about $0.95 per mile on fuel. Diesel can differ by more than $2 a gallon between the cheapest and most expensive states, so where you fuel up matters.
- [Box Truck Dispatch: How to Find Loads and What It Really Costs](https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/box-truck-loads-and-costs/): Box truck owner-operators find loads through load boards, direct broker relationships and dispatch services. A 26 ft diesel box truck typically gets about 8.5-11 mpg. Texas Solutions dispatches box trucks and straight trucks for 8% of weekly gross, OTR, with no flat rate.
